lines.text: Build the identical rows two ways: once as a row-major table, and once as a column-major table split into one separate buffer per column.
Scanning just one of those columns, does the column-major table genuinely touch fewer bytes than the row-major one does?
Yes, genuinely.
Far fewer bytes, in the column-major table.
Run it for real: the column-major table touched far fewer bytes scanning that one column than the row-major table did.
A row-major layout's other columns ride along for free during a narrow scan, so every row's full set of fields gets touched regardless.
Now update every field of one single logical row instead, in each of the two layouts.
Does the column-major table touch more separate, non-adjacent regions doing that than the row-major table does?
Yes, genuinely.
Several separate regions, in the column-major table.
Run it for real: the column-major table touched four separate regions updating that one row, while the row-major table touched exactly one.
Mark every seventh row's own value absent, using a packed bitmap, a single bit per row, the way a real columnar format does it.
Does a scan over that column correctly skip exactly the rows that bitmap marks absent?
Yes, genuinely.
Exactly those rows get skipped.
Run it for real: the scan correctly skipped exactly the rows the bitmap marked absent, using a single bit, not a whole byte, for each one.
A real production columnar format's own documentation states this exact trade-off directly.
Does it name comparatively more expensive mutation as the real cost of its own locality and performance guarantees?
Yes, genuinely.
It names the more expensive mutation cost directly.

lines.text: That format's own documentation states it in exactly those words: real analytical performance and real data locality guarantees, in exchange for comparatively more expensive mutation operations.
That same format's own Rust implementation names the identical trade-off from the other side, the implementation side.
Handling the validity bitmap on its own, separately from each value, is named directly as a real, measured performance improvement over folding it in.

So here's the shape of this whole topic: a column-major layout genuinely touches far fewer bytes scanning a single column, and its packed bitmap genuinely skips exactly the rows it marks absent, at a small fraction of a byte-per-row's own cost.

What it pays for that is real: updating every field of one single logical row now means touching several separate, non-adjacent buffers instead of one contiguous region, the way a row-major layout would.
That's the real trade a columnar format makes on purpose, stated directly in its own documentation: cheap scanning, bought with expensive mutation.
